precepts.text: This is Jacob talking: twenty years have I been with thee; that which was torn of beasts I brought not unto thee; I bare the loss of it. In the day the drought consumed me, and the frost by night. I served thee fourteen years for thy two daughters, and six years for thy cattle: and thou hast changed my wages ten times. Laban was a grimy dude, man. He did Jacob dirty: yo, man, you changed my wages, my paycheck is all low, I'm taking care of your cattle, you're doing me wrong over here.
precepts.point: So Jacob was Laban's shepherd. He took care of the sheep, the cattle. He was a shepherd just like Abel was a shepherd, and Esau was the man of the field just like Cain was a man of the field. You see where I'm going with this?

note.label: As in the Days of Noah: Past & Present

precepts.why:
Rebekah told Jacob to flee to her brother Laban's house because Esau wanted him dead, so he ran to Laban, and “Jacob fed the rest of Laban’s flocks.” He took rods of green poplar, hazel and chesnut, “pilled white strakes in them,” and set them before the flocks at the watering troughs. The stronger cattle conceived among the rods, “so the feebler were Laban’s, and the stronger Jacob’s.” “And the man increased exceedingly.”

So Jacob was Laban's shepherd; he took care of the sheep and the cattle. He was a shepherd just as Abel was a shepherd, and Esau was the man of the field just as Cain was a man of the field. The same two lines keep repeating.

And Jacob tells what that shepherding cost him: “This twenty years have I been with thee;” “That which was torn of beasts I brought not unto thee; I bare the loss of it.” “Thus I was; in the day the drought consumed me, and the frost by night; and my sleep departed from mine eyes.” “I served thee fourteen years for thy two daughters, and six years for thy cattle: and thou hast changed my wages ten times.”

Laban was a grimy man. He did Jacob dirty: Jacob took care of his cattle day and night, bore the losses himself, and Laban kept lowering his pay. Yet God increased Jacob exceedingly in spite of it.

precepts.text: Rachel demanded children and Jacob asked, Am I in God's stead? The same answer to sisters demanding a lord from leadership: go ask God for it, and ask what he wants you to change first.
precepts.point: This kind can come forth by nothing but by prayer and fasting. Some demons are higher than others, and that is why you have to fast and pray and not let it conquer you. God put leadership in your life to watch over your soul; instead of pointing at them, fix yourself, be the Proverbs 31 woman, stop eating the ice cream at night, and earn it rather than assume you deserve it.

note.label: A Soul Without Purpose

precepts.why:
When Rachel wanted a child and came demanding one from Jacob, “Jacob’s anger was kindled against Rachel: and he said, Am I in God’s stead, who hath withheld from thee the fruit of the womb?” Jacob could not give what only God gives. Go ask God for that baby.

That is the same answer for the single sister who points at leadership because she has been here five, six, seven years and has no lord, while a sister who came after her already has one. Leadership is not in God’s stead. If you want a lord, go ask God, and ask him what he wants you to change first. Check yourself: maybe talk to the sister who came after you and ask how she did it, instead of calling it hatred from leadership. God put leadership in your life to watch over your soul. Be the Proverbs 31 woman, fix your mouth, do the work on the body, stop eating the ice cream at night, and know your size before you point at the fit brother. It is not something you deserve; it is something you earn, by sacrifice.

The same dumb spirit Christ cast out of the boy tells that sister to go into the world, get a lord, and bring him in, when in the world she caught nothing before. Go into the world and you are still the same negro, still the same woman; you never changed, because you would not go to the Lord. Some came here for the ride and not the work. One sister reached out to a man in the world, and he is gone; another left for a man online who said he did not believe in two or three wives, then found out he did. Some of you are not going to get a lord in this captivity, and if that is what you came for, Satan will move you out of the way.

That spirit is the one that “ofttimes” cast the child “into the fire, and into the waters, to destroy him”: the paycheck spent in the club that gets sprayed up, the drunk drive that costs your limbs, the mob on Eastern Parkway, in the mix of a bunch of no-good negroes up to no good. Leaving your house to go with the dumb negroes is a dumb spirit. We thought it was cool; it was a dumb and deaf spirit, not listening and not seeing our condition. “If thou canst believe, all things are possible to him that believeth”: your belief is your power. When Satan keeps attacking you, your faith is weak, so cry like the father, “Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief.”

“This kind can come forth by nothing, but by prayer and fasting.” Some demons are higher than others, so fast and pray, and do not let it conquer you. And once made whole, hear Christ: “sin no more, lest a worse thing come unto thee.” The world you left two years ago is not the world you would go back to; sin has multiplied, and worse demons are jumping on people.

precepts.text: They that marry have not sinned, but such shall have trouble in the flesh; in marriage there will be some hard times.
precepts.point: Their arguing is the trouble in the flesh the scriptures speak of. If thou marry, thou hast not sinned, but such shall have trouble in the flesh: it is not all going to be sweet all the time. Rachel's trouble in the flesh was that she envied her sister and could not bear children, and she took it out on Jacob.

note.label: Genesis 30: Trouble in the Flesh and a Righteous Hire

precepts.why:
“But and if thou marry, thou hast not sinned; and if a virgin marry, she hath not sinned. Nevertheless such shall have trouble in the flesh: but I spare you.” They that marry have not sinned, but such shall have trouble in the flesh; in marriage there will be some hard times. It is not all going to be sweet all the time.

Rachel and Jacob arguing is that trouble in the flesh. Rachel saw that she bare Jacob no children, envied her sister, and said, “Give me children, or else I die.” Jacob's anger was kindled: “Am I in God’s stead, who hath withheld from thee the fruit of the womb?” Jacob was not the problem; he was having no trouble producing children. Rachel's trouble in the flesh was that she envied her sister and could not bear children, and she took it out on Jacob.

precepts.text: Praise ye the Lord, O ye servants of the Lord; blessed be the name of the Lord from this time forth and for evermore.
precepts.point: It was not the mandrakes that gave her the child; it is only coincidence that the baby came after she had them. The Most High is the one who showed her mercy and opened up her womb, for he maketh the barren woman to keep house and to be a joyful mother of children.

note.label: Genesis 30: Trouble in the Flesh and a Righteous Hire

precepts.why:
“Praise ye the Lord. Praise, O ye servants of the Lord, praise the name of the Lord. Blessed be the name of the Lord from this time forth and for evermore.”

That is the answer to Rachel's son. “God remembered Rachel, and God hearkened to her, and opened her womb”, and she said, “God hath taken away my reproach”. It was not the mandrakes that gave her the child; it is only coincidence that the baby came after she had them. The Most High showed her mercy and opened her womb, and the praise for it belongs to His name.

precepts.text: He maketh the barren woman to keep house and to be a joyful mother of children; the Most High is the one who opened Rachel's womb.
precepts.point: It was not the mandrakes that gave her the child; it is only coincidence that the baby came after she had them. The Most High is the one who showed her mercy and opened up her womb, for he maketh the barren woman to keep house and to be a joyful mother of children.

note.label: Genesis 30: Trouble in the Flesh and a Righteous Hire

precepts.why:
“He maketh the barren woman to keep house, and to be a joyful mother of children. Praise ye the Lord.”

Rachel was barren, and it was not the mandrakes that changed that; it is only coincidence that the baby came after she had them. The Most High is the one who showed her mercy and opened up her womb: “God remembered Rachel, and God hearkened to her, and opened her womb”, and she bare Joseph and said, “God hath taken away my reproach”. He is the one who makes the barren woman a joyful mother of children.

precepts.text: After the war Abram told the king of Sodom, I will not take from a thread even to a shoelatchet, lest thou shouldest say, I have made Abram rich; the Most High was his provider, and that is the spirit of the forefathers.
precepts.point: Laban agreed, then removed that same day the he goats that were ringstraked and spotted, all the speckled and spotted she goats, and the brown among the sheep, and gave them into the hand of his own sons, setting three days' journey between himself and Jacob.

note.label: Genesis 30: Trouble in the Flesh and a Righteous Hire

precepts.why:
After the war, “the king of Sodom said unto Abram, Give me the persons, and take the goods to thyself.” Abram refused: “I have lift up mine hand unto the Lord, the most high God, the possessor of heaven and earth, That I will not take from a thread even to a shoelatchet, and that I will not take any thing that is thine, lest thou shouldest say, I have made Abram rich”. The Most High was his provider, and no man was going to say he made Abram rich.

Jacob has the same spirit when Laban asks, “What shall I give thee?” “Thou shalt not give me any thing”. He asked no gift, only terms: he would keep feeding Laban's flock, and the speckled, spotted and brown among the sheep and goats from that day forward would be his hire. And he set terms that could be checked in the open: “So shall my righteousness answer for me in time to come”, and every one that was not speckled and spotted among the goats and brown among the sheep would “be counted stolen with me.” Judge me on my works; my word is my bond. He said it because he knew they were going to have something bad to say about his increase.

That refusal is the spirit our forefathers rolled in, Abram and Jacob alike. We have to come back to these scriptures and to the understanding of who we are, because our people are lost and have fainted from that spirit. We cannot roll in a handout spirit; when we repent we have to conduct ourselves as men and provide for our own houses, for the Most High provides.

precepts.text: Rachel said to Jacob, Give me children, or else I die; that is how heavy childlessness sat upon our foremothers, and that is why Jephthah's daughter bewailed her virginity.
precepts.point: And it was a custom in Israel, that the daughters of Israel went yearly to lament the daughter of Jephthah the Gileadite four days in a year.

note.label: Judges 11: Jephthah and the Search of the Fathers

precepts.why:
Why would Jephthah’s daughter bewail her virginity if she were about to die? Because the sorrow was that she could never marry or bear children. See how heavy childlessness sat upon our foremothers: “when Rachel saw that she bare Jacob no children, Rachel envied her sister; and said unto Jacob, Give me children, or else I die.” And Jacob answered, “Am I in God’s stead, who hath withheld from thee the fruit of the womb?”

In those days our women wanted to bring children into the world and continue the lineage; to be without children was counted a shame and a dishonour among the daughters of Israel. Rachel would rather die than be without children. So the daughter of Jephthah, her life now vowed to the Lord, went with her companions and bewailed her virginity upon the mountains: not her death, but that she would never know a man.

She returned unto her father, he did with her according to his vow, “and she knew no man.” If she had been put to death there would be no reason for the scripture to say she knew no man. Israel did not do human sacrifices; that was Molech worship among the Canaanites. She was presented to the Lord to serve him, and she remained a virgin.

precepts.text: Laban said, I have learned by experience that the Lord hath blessed me for thy sake; Laban knew where his blessings came from, for he had little before Jacob arrived and increased while our forefather served him.
precepts.point: Does that mean she would inherit the kingdom as a Moabitess? No. She joined herself under Israel and acknowledged her place in the hierarchy under Israel, and the scriptures give examples of strangers who did the same.

note.label: Ruth 1: Naomi and Ruth Return from Moab

precepts.why:
Laban also knew where his blessings came from. “And Laban said unto him, I pray thee, if I have found favour in thine eyes, tarry: for I have learned by experience that the Lord hath blessed me for thy sake.”

Laban had little before Jacob arrived and increased while our forefather served him, and he learned by experience that the Lord blessed him for Jacob's sake. Ruth saw the same in Naomi: whither thou goest, I will go, because the blessing is with Israel and Israel's God.

precepts.text: Laban confesses he has learned by experience that the Most High blessed him for Jacob's sake, as the nations are blessed for Israel's sake today.
precepts.point: We are living this now. Every time a foreign king came up to invade Israel he stripped the silver and gold and pleasant things out of the temple and exacted tribute. In this captivity Esau still profits off our labour and our inventions, the light filament, the plasma and open heart surgery, the cotton gin, computers and cell phones, yet makes no account of who produced them.

note.label: Proverbs 5: The Strange Woman and Thy Labours in the House of a Stranger

precepts.why:
“Lest strangers be filled with thy wealth; and thy labours be in the house of a stranger”. Jacob's labours were in the house of Laban, and Laban knew what he was getting from it: “And Laban said unto him, I pray thee, if I have found favour in thine eyes, tarry: for I have learned by experience that the Lord hath blessed me for thy sake.”

Laban confesses he has learned by experience that the Most High blessed him for Jacob's sake. The stranger was filled with wealth because Israel was laboring in his house.

That is how the nations are blessed for Israel's sake today. Esau profits off our labour and our inventions in this captivity and makes no account of who produced them, but like Laban, the blessing came for Jacob's sake.

A very beautiful woman can be very manipulative and use her beauty to control you; Eve did that to Adam, and here the same thing is being done to Jacob. note.label: Leaven: The Root of Bitterness

points: And Jacob's anger was kindled against Rachel: and he said, Am I in God's stead, who hath withheld from thee the fruit of the womb? This is an argument Moses saw between Jacob and his wife, and he wrote it down in a kosher way for us. Jacob was angry, and when a man is angry he lifts his voice. That is not abuse. Sisters, when your husband gets angry and yells and corrects you, that is not abuse; take the correction, see what he is saying, and fix it, instead of trying to justify yourself. Because when a woman tries to justify herself, Satan comes in her mind saying, he was wrong for what he said to you, that is abuse right there; and if you listen to Satan, you end up divorced. A sister called the teacher this same week saying her husband was abusive; when she explained, it was arguments, and some things the brother should not have said, but it was still not abuse. Abuse is abuse, and correction is not it.
